claims.claim: France's April 17, 1825 ordinance demanded Haiti pay 150 million francs, in five annual installments, to compensate former colonists claiming an indemnity.
claims.verbatim: Les habitans actuels de la partie française de Saint-Domingue verseront à la caisse générale des dépôts et consignations de France, en cinq termes égaux, d'année en année, le premier échéant au 31 décembre 1825, la somme de cent cinquante millions de francs, destinée à dédommager les anciens colons qui réclameront une indemnité.

claims.claim: The 1825 ordinance's payments were meant to compensate former colonists for lost property, meaning most notably the formerly enslaved Haitians themselves.
claims.verbatim: The payments were to compensate the former colonists who would claim compensation for the loss of their property (meaning, most notably, the formerly enslaved Haitians themselves).

claims.claim: In July 1825 France sent a fleet of 14 warships carrying 528 cannons to enforce the indemnity demand.
France's emissary was instructed to threaten a blockade that would continue until Haiti submitted itself, without any conditions, to the supremacy of France.
claims.verbatim: submitted itself, without any conditions, to the supremacy of France

claims.claim: Historians argue the French gunboats represented not just a threat of force but the potential threat of re-enslavement.
claims.verbatim: The French gunboats did not merely represent a threat of force but the potential threat of reenslavement.

claims.claim: By 1789, Saint-Domingue produced three-quarters of the world's sugar and 60 percent of France and Britain's coffee, making it the world's richest colony.
claims.verbatim: Saint Domingue led the world in production of [sugar, coffee, cotton, indigo] at one time or another during the eighteenth century... By 1789, sixty percent of France and Britain's coffee and three-quarters of the world's sugar came from Saint Domingue. It was the world's richest colony and the busiest trade center in the New World.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 3: Richest Colony in the World

claims.claim: Haiti is the only state founded and sustained by enslaved people who won their freedom by force of arms.
claims.verbatim: Haiti... remains the only state founded and sustained by slaves who won their freedom by force of arms.

claims.claim: Of the roughly 33,000 troops Napoleon sent to reconquer Saint-Domingue, about 30,000 died.
In 1838, France reduced Haiti's outstanding indemnity balance to 60 million francs, for a total indemnity of 90 million instead of 150 million.
claims.verbatim: [The 1838 treaty] reduced the outstanding amount owed to sixty million francs, for a total indemnity of ninety million instead of 150 million.

claims.claim: Haiti's insolvency on the indemnity was already patent by its second payment deadline, at the end of 1826.
claims.verbatim: patent as of the second payment deadline, at the end of 1826

claims.claim: Haiti took 122 years, from 1825 to 1947, to repay its independence debt, with final payments going to the National City Bank.
claims.verbatim: It took Haiti 122 years to repay its Independence Debt... All of Haiti's outstanding debts to French banks were acquired by the National City Bank in 1922. Payments in service of those debts, begun in 1825, continued until 1947.

claims.claim: The New York Times calculated Haiti paid roughly $560 million in today's dollars over the 64 years of indemnity payments it tracked.
claims.verbatim: The Times tracked each payment Haiti made over the course of 64 years, and calculated that Haiti ended up paying about $560 million in today's dollars.

claims.claim: By 1898, half of Haiti's government budget went to debt service to France; by 1914, that share had risen to 80 percent.
claims.verbatim: By 1898, fully half of Haiti's government budget went to paying France and the French banks. By 1914, that proportion had climbed to 80 percent.

claims.claim: Because so much of Haiti's budget went to debt service, education, healthcare and infrastructure went practically unfunded throughout the nineteenth century.
claims.verbatim: Education, healthcare and infrastructure went practically unfunded throughout the Nineteenth Century.

claims.claim: While the bank financing Haiti's debt was also helping finance the Eiffel Tower, its executives sometimes made more profit off Haiti than Haiti's entire public works budget.
claims.verbatim: At a time when the bank, known as C.I.C., was helping finance the Eiffel Tower, its executives and investors made so much money off Haiti that their profits sometimes exceeded Haiti's entire public works budget.

claims.claim: Investors in the National Bank of Haiti cleared an average 15 percent annual return, triple the roughly 5 percent typical of French investments at the time.
claims.verbatim: At a time when many French investment returns hovered around 5 percent, investors in the National Bank of Haiti cleared an average of 15 percent per year.

claims.claim: Estimates of Haiti's total economic loss from the indemnity range from $21 billion to $115 billion depending on methodology, with Piketty valuing it at roughly 40 billion euros.
claims.source: Daut p.267, NYT "The Ransom", Piketty p.217

claims.claim: Factoring in what the indemnity money could have done for Haiti's economy over centuries, losses could total as much as $115 billion, many times the size of Haiti's economy today.
claims.verbatim: Factor in what that money could have done to Haiti's economy over the course of centuries, and it comes out to as much as $115 billion in losses for Haiti over time—many times the size of its entire economy today.

claims.claim: Haiti became the world's only country where the descendants of enslaved people paid reparations to the descendants of their masters, and for generations.
claims.verbatim: Haiti became the world's only country where the descendants of enslaved people paid reparations to the descendants of their masters, and for generations.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 11: Only Country Where Slaves Paid Masters

claims.claim: When Britain abolished slavery it paid roughly 20 million pounds, 5 percent of national income, directly to about 4,000 slaveowners rather than making the formerly enslaved pay.
claims.verbatim: Some 20 million pounds sterling, or 5 percent of the UK's national income at the time, was paid to some 4,000 slaveowners.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 11: Only Country Where Slaves Paid Masters

claims.claim: In 2003, Haitian President Aristide formally demanded France repay $21,685,135,571.48, calculated from the 90-million-franc indemnity plus 5 percent annual interest.
claims.verbatim: France owes Haiti U.S.$21,685,135,571.48 and counting, at five percent annual interest.

claims.claim: Aristide argued France extorted the indemnity money from Haiti by force and should return it to fund schools, health care, water systems, and roads.
claims.verbatim: France extorted this money from Haiti by force and you should give it back to us so that we can build primary schools, primary health care, water systems, and roads.

claims.claim: France's official position, restated by a Foreign Ministry spokesman in 2004, is that the reparations case has been closed since 1885.
claims.verbatim: [T]his case has been closed since 1885.

claims.claim: In 2015, President Hollande said France owed Haiti a moral debt but that financial or monetary reparations were out of the question.
claims.verbatim: To be sure, France owed Haiti a sort of 'moral' debt, but it was out of the question even to consider any kind of financial or monetary reparations.

claims.claim: The regime that removed President Aristide on February 29, 2004 renounced Haiti's reparations claim within its first week in power.
claims.verbatim: The appointed coup regime renounced the claim within its first week in power.

claims.claim: Economist Lundahl argues Haiti's later foreign debts of 1874-1896 resulted mainly from corrupt domestic politicians rather than the earlier indemnity or neocolonial exploitation.
claims.verbatim: The 1825 indemnity continued to lay a heavy hand on the Haitian economy for several decades, but it is not correct to contend that it was the main cause of the new foreign loans assumed in 1874, 1875, and 1896... These loans were not the result of neocolonial exploitation, but rather of corrupt domestic politicians mortgaging Haiti's development possibilities in order to fill their own pockets.

claims.claim: The 1825 ordinance amounted to an international exchange of cash for human lives and their value as slave labor, which French law and international norms at the time condemned.
claims.verbatim: The 1825 Ordinance... represented an international transaction exchanging cash for human lives and their value as slave labor. French law and international treaties and norms condemned such an agreement.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 16: Debt Was Illegal Even in 1825

claims.claim: A later French legal report, the Dalloz Report, declared the original 1825 ordinance unlawful and placed liability for colonists' losses with the French government itself.
claims.verbatim: The Dalloz Report declared the original Ordinance unlawful and placed liability for the colonists' losses with the French government itself.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 16: Debt Was Illegal Even in 1825

claims.claim: By contemporary legal standards, the Haitian indemnity qualifies as an odious debt, imposed by a despotic regime lacking popular consent, providing no benefit to the populace, with lenders aware of these facts.
claims.verbatim: Judged by contemporary standards, it is easy to see the case as one involving an odious debt. The term refers to a debt incurred by a regime that lacked popular consent (a 'despotic' regime), provided no benefit to the populace where the lenders had reason to know of these facts.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 16: Debt Was Illegal Even in 1825

claims.claim: In 1947, Haitian President Dumarsais Estimé completed the final indemnity-linked debt payment, calling it Haiti's financial emancipation.
claims.verbatim: financial emancipation

claims.claim: Repaying the 1922 U.S. loan led to the withdrawal of the U.S. financial adviser and the Haitianization of Haiti's national bank.
claims.verbatim: [The repayment of the U.S. loan of 1922 led to the withdrawal of the U.S. financial adviser and the Haitianization of the national bank.]

claims.claim: France's indemnity process legitimized 25,838 colonist claimants, adjudicating 10,345 properties, with the top 86 recipients receiving 1,512 to 3,396 francs and the bottom 9,450 receiving as little as 1 to 7.50 francs each.
claims.verbatim: [9,450 colons auront à recevoir... les uns 1 fr., 2 fr., 3 fr., 4 fr., et jusqu'à 7 fr. 50 c.]

claims.claim: France's indemnity scheme classified the formerly enslaved people as biens immeubles, or immovable property, the same legal category as land, using it to calculate colonist payouts.
claims.verbatim: The formerly enslaved people were classed as biens immeubles (immovable property). They... '[ne pouvaient être saisis indépendamment des propriétés foncières]' and served as the primary basis for estimating the payouts.

claims.claim: Journalist Félix Darfour was arrested for sedition, tried in a military court despite being a civilian, and executed after accusing President Boyer of having sold the country to the whites through the indemnity agreement.
claims.verbatim: Darfour wrote to the Chamber of Deputies, accusing Boyer of having '[sold the country to the whites]' through the indemnity agreement... Darfour was arrested for sedition and tried in a military court despite being a civilian. He was '[sentenced to death and executed].'

claims.claim: Boyer's own advisory commission rejected the French ordinance text immediately upon reading it in July 1825.
claims.verbatim: [The members of the commission, shocked by what they read, rejected the document immediately and categorically.]

claims.claim: Boyer withheld the actual royal ordinance text from a subsequent private council, letting its members believe the document matched his previous, milder instructions.
claims.verbatim: Boyer had not communicated to the members of this private council, the copy he held of the royal ordinance... he was able to induce them to think that the one presented... contained, more or less, the clauses carried in [his previous] instructions.

claims.claim: After the Haitian Senate approved the indemnity agreement, the document was locked away in a velvet case rather than made public.
claims.verbatim: [The Haitian Senate registered approval of the agreement after hearing it read publicly to them; then the document was locked away in a velvet case.]

claims.claim: Haitians only discovered months later, from newspapers arriving from France, that Boyer had contracted a massive multigenerational debt without consulting the citizens of his country.
claims.verbatim: [It was only several months later, when newspapers describing the agreement arrived from France, that Haitians found out that—without consulting the citizens of his country—Boyer had contracted a massive debt, one they would have to pay for generations.]

claims.claim: In December 1914, U.S. Marines from the USS Machias entered the Banque Nationale d'Haïti and removed $500,000 in gold belonging to the Haitian government, shipping it to New York.
claims.verbatim: In December 1914, the USS Machias dropped anchor in the harbor of Port-au-Prince and a detachment of U.S. marines disembarked. They proceeded to carry out what can only be described as an international armed robbery. Entering the Banque Nationale d'Haïti, they removed from the vaults $500,000 worth of gold belonging to the Haitian government—the equivalent of $11 million today. Then, in broad daylight, they took the gold back to the harbor, loaded it onto their gunboat, and shipped it to New York.

claims.claim: Roger Farnham simultaneously served as vice president of New York's National City Bank and vice president of the Banque Nationale d'Haïti, whose flag was changed from the French tricolor to the Stars and Stripes.
claims.verbatim: Roger Farnham, the vice president of the National City Bank in New York, took on the additional title of vice president for the Banque Nationale, and the French tricolor that had flown in front of the bank since its founding was soon replaced with the Stars and Stripes.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 28: Roger Farnham Dual VP / Conflict of Interest

claims.claim: Roger Farnham told U.S. Secretary of State Bryan that Haiti's financial situation constitutes a certain form of slavery for the masses.
claims.verbatim: constitutes a certain form of slavery for the masses
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 28: Roger Farnham Dual VP / Conflict of Interest

claims.claim: U.S. Marine General Smedley Butler said he helped make Haiti and Cuba a decent place for the National City Bank boys to collect revenues in.
claims.verbatim: I helped make Haiti and Cuba a decent place for the National City Bank boys to collect revenues in.

claims.claim: France's envoy Mackau was instructed that his mission was not a negotiation and that he lacked the power to modify the ordinance's terms at all.
claims.verbatim: My mission to the people of our former colony is not a negotiation... I lack the powers to make the slightest modification

claims.claim: Mackau's instructions said that if Haiti refused the ordinance, he was to announce that its leaders would thereafter be treated as enemies of France.
claims.verbatim: Announce to the leaders of that government that henceforth they will be treated as enemies of France

claims.claim: The 150-million-franc indemnity figure equaled Saint-Domingue's former annual colonial revenue and represented only about a tenth of the 1789 value of its immovable property.
claims.verbatim: Le chiffre de l'indemnité, identique à celui des revenus annuels de l'ancienne colonie, ne représente donc que « la dixième partie seulement de la valeur, en 1789, des biens immeubles... »

claims.claim: Boyer's secret council was asked whether France could reserve for French commerce a rate of only half the duties owed by other nations under the ordinance's first article.
claims.verbatim: Le Roi de France, dans l'acte qui reconnaît l'indépendance du gouvernement d'Haïti, peut-il, dans le premier article, déclarer que les ports du pays sont ouverts au commerce de toutes les nations, en réservant pour le commerce français l'avantage de n'être assujetti qu'à la moitié des droits auxquels les autres sont tenus?

claims.claim: An American newspaper argued that by purchasing acknowledgment of an already undisputed fact, Boyer cast doubt on whether Haiti could actually keep the independence it had begged to buy.
claims.verbatim: One effect of this foolish treaty—foolish only on the part of Boyer—is, that by purchasing the acknowledgment of what was before an undisputed fact, he has brought the fact itself into question, for he has afforded room to doubt, that Haiti had the means of keeping that which she had begged herself to buy.

claims.claim: When a Haitian senator proposed a toast to abolitionist ally Abbé Grégoire, the visiting French delegation set down their glasses in visible disapproval.
claims.verbatim: posed their glasses on the table, with a visible sentiment of improbation

claims.claim: Poet and independence propagandist Chanlatte came from a huge family of enslavers on both his mother's and his father's side.
claims.verbatim: from a huge family of enslavers on both his mother's and his father's side

claims.claim: At an 1826 dinner, Chanlatte sang a song praising King Charles X as a philosopher and lover of liberty, despite Charles X having just extracted Haiti's indemnity.
Banker Pierre Paravey used his position financing the Haitian indemnity to enter the financial circles of Rothschild and Laffitte and make his bank a shareholder of the Banque de France.
claims.verbatim: With their support, Pierre Paravey managed to enter the main financial circles (those including Rothschild and Laffitte) and have the bank become a shareholder of the Banque de France.
claims.anchor: ✅ CLAIM 36: Paravey Bank → Banque de France

claims.claim: President Estimé pleaded with the U.S. government to forgive Haiti's remaining debt but was refused, leaving his reform ambitions underfunded by continuing debt payments.
claims.verbatim: Estimé pleaded with the U.S. government to forgive the debt, but to no avail, and with Haiti's state budget sapped by debt payments, many of Estimé's ambitious ideas remained nothing more than that.

claims.claim: Domestic opposition to the indemnity was one of the causes of the 1843 revolution that forced President Boyer into exile.
claims.verbatim: The domestic opposition to the indemnity [was] one of the causes of the 1843 revolution which forced President Boyer into exile.

claims.claim: The 1844 Piquets uprising, led by Jean-Jacques Acaau, demanded cancelling the indemnity being paid to France.
claims.verbatim: Cancelling the indemnity being paid to France

claims.claim: Three named members of the French Parliament, Alexandre Delaborde, Emmanuel de Las Cases, and François-André Isambert, publicly denounced the amounts Haiti was required to pay.
claims.verbatim: Members of the parliament such as Alexandre Delaborde, Emmanuel de Las Cases, and François-André Isambert denounced the amounts to be paid.

claims.claim: Members of both French legislative chambers knew nothing about the Haiti independence negotiations and learned Haiti had been granted independence only from the press.
claims.verbatim: Members of the two French Chambers, the Chambre des Pairs and the Chambre des Députés, knew nothing about the negotiations and discovered in the press that Haiti had been granted its independence.
